rows.q: Who is the mayor of Squamish?
rows.answer:
Squamish's mayor is **Sean Easton**. He won the general election on October 17, 2026, and the new council was due to be sworn in at its first meeting on November 3, 2026.

Final results confirmed by the District of Squamish:
- **Sean Easton**: 3,681 votes (elected)
- Jenna Stoner: 3,506 votes
- Daniel Deal: 1,591 votes

Voter turnout was about 45%, up from about 41% in 2022. Easton replaces Armand Hurford, who was elected mayor in 2022.

rows.q: Where can I easily follow what Squamish council decides at each meeting?
rows.answer:
The easiest place is the **District of Squamish Council Portal**, which runs on CivicWeb:
👉 **https://squamish.civicweb.net/Portal/**

It describes itself as the one place for council meeting videos, schedules, agendas and minutes. In practice:

- **Before a meeting:** Read the agenda and staff reports so you know what's coming up for a decision.
- **After a meeting:** Read the minutes. They record every motion, who moved and seconded it, and whether it passed. This is the official record of decisions. For an example, see the minutes from June 17, 2025 (https://squamish.civicweb.net/document/255150/).
- **Video:** Open council meetings are streamed live, and recordings are kept, so you can watch the discussion as well as the vote.
- **Search:** You can search recent and past agendas, minutes and video. There's also a Document Centre with council correspondence, bylaws and policies.

You can also get to the portal from the District's main website, **squamish.ca**. Look for "View Council Agendas, Minutes, Videos, Bylaws & Policies." That section also explains how to speak at a public hearing or appear before council.

**Tips:**
- Minutes are usually posted only after council approves them at the next meeting. For the latest decisions, the video or local news is often faster.

rows.q: What did Sean Easton promise when he ran for mayor of Squamish?
rows.answer:
Sean Easton ran for mayor of Squamish in the October 2026 election on three themes: **affordability, accessibility and accountability**. He won on October 17, 2026, with 3,681 votes (41.9%). Jenna Stoner came second with 3,506, a margin of 175 votes.

His main promises were:

**Affordable living**
- **Freeze property taxes for 2027.** This was his best-known pledge. He argued that the District spends too much on projects and staff.
- Build housing that locals can afford throughout their lives.
- Invest in modernized transportation that meets different needs.
- Spend taxpayers' money transparently and in ways that deliver real results.

**Accessible amenities**
- Push the provincial and federal governments to give Squamish its fair share of funding.
- Improve access to recreational, cultural and arts amenities, and to social and health services for all ages.

**Accountable leadership**
- Keep engaging with residents in an ongoing, meaningful way.
- Be fully transparent about how the District uses its resources. He said residents told him they didn't feel heard or believe their tax dollars were being spent well.
- Cut red tape. CBC described his campaign as focused on freezing taxes and cutting red tape.

He ran as an independent with the slogan "A Mayor for the Community." He has lived in Squamish since 2011 and co-founded the non-profits Zero Ceiling and DWIFT Housing.

rows.q: How do I speak at a Squamish council meeting?
rows.answer:
There are two main ways to speak at a District of Squamish council meeting. You can book a spot ahead of time as a delegation, or you can speak briefly during the meeting without booking.

## Option 1: Apply to appear as a delegation (best for getting time on the agenda)
1. **Put your request in writing.** If you want Council to consider an issue, you have to send a written request with all the relevant details. Address it to **Mayor and Council, District of Squamish**.
2. **Say that you want to speak.** If you want to present in person, your written request has to say so.
3. **Use the "Application to Appear" form.** You can download it from the District's Council Meetings page (squamish.ca → Government & Administration → Council → Council Meetings & Public Notices) or from the "Participating in Meetings" section of the CivicWeb portal (squamish.civicweb.net).
4. If your request is approved, you'll be listed under "Delegations" on the meeting agenda.

## Option 2: Unscheduled Public Attendance (no booking needed)
Regular meetings include an "Unscheduled Public Attendance" segment. The Mayor explains the rules under Procedure Bylaw No. 3032, 2024, then asks if anyone in the room wants to speak. You can come forward, say which agenda item you're speaking to, and address Council for a few minutes. Recent minutes show five-minute speaking slots.

## Meeting details
- **Where and when:** Regular Business Meetings start at **6 p.m.** in Council Chambers, Municipal Hall, 37955 Secon

rows.q: How much are Squamish councillors and the mayor paid?
rows.answer:
Need recent figures.I couldn't find current (2026) dollar figures. My search tool hit its usage limit, so I'm working from older official documents. Here's what they show.

**How pay is set (District of Squamish Bylaw No. 1503, as amended)**
- **Mayor:** The annual remuneration for the Mayor is $85,421, effective January 1, 2019. Starting that date, it is adjusted each January in line with the District of Squamish Exempt Salary Policy.
- **Councillors:** A councillor's annual pay is 42.2% of the Mayor's, adjusted each year to keep that ratio. In 2019 that worked out to about **$36,050** per councillor (my calculation).

**What it was before**
A 2016 district compensation review listed the Mayor's pay at $67,194.40 and a councillor's at $28,901.60. The review also found that the District of Squamish Mayor was being paid 13% less than the average annual remuneration for full time Mayors in comparable communities. The 2019 raise followed that review.

**Today's pay**
Because of the yearly adjustments since 2019, today's amounts will be higher than $85,421 and about $36,050. Councillors should still get 42.2% of whatever the Mayor is paid. For the exact current figures, check:
- the District's latest **Statement of Financial Information (SOFI)**, which lists what each elected official was actually paid and their expenses each year, or
- the consolidated Bylaw 1503 on squamish.ca, or the District's finance department.

rows.q: How did Squamish council vote on the Woodfibre LNG tax deal?
rows.answer:
Squamish council **voted 5–2 to reject** the Woodfibre LNG tax deal at a special meeting on September 22, 2026.

**What the deal was:** It was a 10-year arrangement, made up of a community enhancement payment agreement (CEPA) and revitalized tax exemption (RTE). It would have provided the District with at least $142 million in payments and municipal property taxes, and it would have commenced in 2027.

**How councillors voted:**
- Jenna Stoner put forward a motion to decline the agreement. She said she didn't think it was "a good enough deal for our community".
- Councillors Eric Andersen and John French both were in support of the agreement. French argued that "There is no better agreement out there."
- Those who voted no argued that regular taxation would keep existing protections and allow future councils to decide how to distribute the tax burden as circumstances changed.

**What happens next:** With the agreement declined, the traditional property tax regime will apply to Woodfibre, and the legal proceedings against the District are slated to continue. Woodfibre LNG's CEO, Luke Schauerte, called the rejection "surprising and disappointing." He also said it was the "final" agreement offer there would be from Woodfibre LNG. The vote happened during a municipal election period, and some councillors who voted against the deal are running for re-election.

rows.q: What's the status of the Woodfibre LNG floatels in Squamish?
rows.answer:
As of my latest search, both floatels are moored at the Woodfibre site and housing workers. I couldn't find any 2026 news showing a change to that.

**The two ships**
- **MV Isabelle X (first floatel):** It has been housing workers since June 2024 and holds approximately 650 construction workers. The first floatel is connected to the electricity grid.
- **MV Saga X (second floatel):** It arrived in Squamish on Nov. 27, 2025, and will accommodate 642 construction workers in cabins at a time, along with space for up to 89 on-board staff. The company says it adds up to 900 new trades jobs.

**Approvals**
- The first floatel was controversial. The District of Squamish voted to deny Woodfibre the permit over concerns of women's safety, waste management and other issues, then B.C.'s Environmental Assessment Office stepped in and authorized the ship.
- The second floatel received regulatory approval from the BC Environmental Assessment Office, the Impact Assessment Agency of Canada, and the Squamish Nation in November 2025.
- In 2025 the district changed course: councillors voted 5-2 in favour of supporting a two-year TUP (temporary use permit) for both floatels. The permit came with a $4 million security deposit, plus a $10,000 daily charge per vessel for every day a floatel stays after the permit expires. I worked out from the article's date that the permit was approved around August 2025, so it likely runs out around mid-2027. Please check that date with the District of Squamish.

rows.q: Is Brennan Park in Squamish getting a new pool or ice rink?
rows.answer:
Both are planned, but neither is approved, funded or being built yet.

**The long-term plan:** The District of Squamish says it wants Brennan Park Recreation Centre to eventually include a second ice rink and second pool, as well as new programming and administration space, accessibility upgrades, and energy retrofits. A 2021 facilities plan described a new wellness centre, a second ice rink and a new eight-lane pool at Brennan Park, which would cost an estimated $77 million.

**Timeline:** In late 2024, a District staff member said "Placeholders are in the Financial Plan for the design of a new pool in 2027 and design of a second ice rink in 2028". The new pool would be an eight-lane, 25-meter design. These dates are for starting design work, not construction, and I couldn't find anything confirming they're still the plan today. Staff also warned that the projects compete for money with other needs, such as critical infrastructure, flood protection, and expanding landfill capacity.

**What's been done so far:** The recent work has been renovations. A $21-million project wrapped up this past July, with Phase 2 still to come. The federal grant paying for it didn't cover new facilities: projects such as a new pool or ice rink do not fall within this grant guideline. A Squamish Reporter opinion piece from September noted that the two retrofit projects together cost more than $35 million. rows.answer:

**The plan**
- The District of Squamish plans to introduce paid parking on Cleveland and Second Ave in Downtown Squamish and a resident parking permit program.
- The District says paid parking will improve parking turnover, reduce congestion and encourage people to walk, bike and use transit.
- This goes back to 2023. The 2023 Downtown Parking Study was presented to Council on September 12, and Council passed a motion directing staff to work on paid parking in Downtown Squamish.

**The delay**
In fall 2024, residents were told to expect paid parking by winter 2025. In December 2024, though, council agreed to start with a paid-parking pilot at several tourism spots around town, and that decision pushed downtown paid parking back until 2027. The pilot is meant to let staff gather data and refine the process before paid parking is expanded to the downtown core.

**The pilot**
Paid parking is now in effect at Darrell Bay on the west side of Highway 99. It's a pilot project currently scheduled to run until the end of 2026. The rates are $3/hr up to $10/day in the peak summer months (June through September) and $1/hr up to $5/day off-peak (October through May).

rows.q: What is Squamish doing about flood protection and the Cheekeye debris barrier?
rows.answer:
I could only partly answer this. The search tool hit its usage limit after one query, so the barrier details below come from one CBC article from about seven months ago (late March 2026). I couldn't check anything more recent or the town's wider flood program.

**Cheekye (also spelled Cheekeye) debris-flow barrier**
- **What it is:** a barrier on the Cheekye River in Brackendale, at the foot of Mount Garibaldi (Nch'ḵay̓). It's about 24 metres tall and built to hold back a debris flow of 2.8 million cubic metres. It's a gravity dam with a 45-degree sloped face: water can flow through, but rocks and debris are held back. CBC put the cost at about $115 million.
- **Who's paying:** the town isn't. A partnership between Squamish Nation and the Squamish developer Matthews West is building it and paying the full cost. The partnership was required to fund it because its Cheekye River housing project (single-family lots, townhouses and commercial space) sits on the Cheekye Fan. That's a fan of sediment built up by past debris flows and floods. The barrier is meant to protect both the new development and the fan as a whole.
- **The town's role:** the District of Squamish will be the local diking authority for the barrier, responsible for funding its operations and maintenance once it's finished.

rows.q: How much does Squamish depend on one large taxpayer like Woodfibre LNG?
rows.answer:
I couldn't find a recent official figure for Woodfibre's share of Squamish's tax revenue. What I found suggests it's meaningful but not overwhelming, and right now the bigger issue is that the amount it will actually pay is in dispute.

**Why it matters**
- Woodfibre LNG is currently the only property in the district that is a Class 4 Major Industry. Squamish has no other major-industry taxpayer to share that burden.
- In 2023, the district's proposed tax rate for Woodfibre was more than four times the B.C. average tax rate for major industry, about $29 per $1,000 assessed value, which would equate to millions of dollars a year.

**The deal that fell through**
- In August 2026 the district put forward an agreement that would guarantee Squamish at least $142 million over a decade. That averages out to about $14 million a year. Under the existing tax approach, the proposed mill rate would have brought an estimated $7.2 million for the 2026 tax year.
